balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

totalIncome.title: Total income
totalIncome.content:
Net interest income plus fees and other operating income.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the top line for a financial; revenue in the ordinary sense does not apply.

What to watch:

  • Income growth versus cost growth

roe.title: Return on equity
roe.content:
ROE is net income as a percentage of average shareholders' equity -- the single number that most directly drives the price-to-book multiple the market will pay.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: ROE has historically run below the larger private-sector peers (ICICI, HDFC) because a meaningful share of consolidated equity sits in subsidiaries (life insurance, asset management, securities) that earn a lower return than the core lending book; annual only, since the CSV carries no reliable quarterly average-equity base.

What to watch:

  • ROE trend versus the cost of equity used in the DCF
  • Whether ROE improvement comes from leverage (capital return) or from margin/NPA improvement

baselRatio.title: Capital adequacy (Basel) ratio
baselRatio.content:
The capital adequacy ratio is total regulatory capital as a percentage of risk-weighted assets, measured against the RBI's Basel III minimum (currently ~11.7% including buffers).

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: the bank runs one of the highest capital ratios among large Indian private banks (low-20s%), which caps ROE but also means growth and buybacks are not capital-constrained the way they are for thinner-capitalised peers.

What to watch:

  • Ratio drifting toward the regulatory minimum as loan growth outpaces retained earnings
  • Capital raises (equity or AT1/Tier-2) that dilute shareholders to rebuild the ratio

bookValue.title: Book value per share
bookValue.content:
Book value per share is shareholders' equity divided by shares outstanding -- the accounting net worth per share, the denominator of the price-to-book ratio.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: for a bank, book value (not revenue or EBITDA) is the natural scale variable; the market typically prices it at a premium to book when ROE exceeds the cost of equity.

What to watch:

  • Book value growth versus ROE (retained earnings should drive most of the increase)
  • Price-to-book relative to the ROE-implied fair multiple

npaRatios.title: Gross and net NPA ratio
npaRatios.content:
Gross NPA ratio is non-performing advances as a percentage of total advances, before provisions. Net NPA ratio deducts provisions already held against those loans -- the residual credit risk still on the balance sheet.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: both ratios sit near the low end of the large private-bank peer group (roughly 1.2% gross / 0.25% net in FY2026), reflecting a loan book still tilted toward secured retail and corporate lending relative to unsecured growth at some peers.

What to watch:

  • Gross NPA rising even one or two quarters in a row -- it leads net NPA and provisioning
  • The gap between gross and net widening (under-provisioning) or narrowing (clean-up)
  • Slippage concentrated in unsecured retail (personal loans, credit cards) where Kotak has been expanding

depositsLoans.title: Deposits vs net loans & advances
depositsLoans.content:
Deposits are the bank's primary funding source; net loans & advances is the lending book, net of provisions. The ratio between them (the credit-deposit ratio) shows how fully deposits are deployed into loans versus held in investments/cash.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: loans and deposits have grown roughly in lockstep (both ~₹5.6-6.5tn through FY2026-FY2027), keeping the credit-deposit ratio broadly stable rather than drawing down liquidity to fund growth.

What to watch:

  • Loan growth materially outpacing deposit growth (forces costlier wholesale/bond funding)
  • CASA mix within deposits (not broken out in this CSV) -- the cheaper the deposit base, the better the margin

preProvision.title: Net interest income, pre-provision profit & credit cost
preProvision.content:
Net interest income (interest earned less interest paid) funds pre-provision operating profit (NII plus fees, less operating costs); the credit impairment charge is what gets deducted from that before tax to reach net income.

For Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited: credit costs have been a small fraction of pre-provision profit through FY2026 (roughly 13%), consistent with the low NPA ratios above; a widening gap between the two lines is usually the first sign of a credit cycle turning before it shows up in the NPA ratios themselves.

What to watch:

  • Credit impairment charge rising as a share of pre-provision profit
  • Pre-provision profit growth versus net interest income growth (operating leverage or cost creep)
